parts.note: without means having no, giving the word no
vices are faults or defects of character

explanation.surface: Racehorses that appear to have no bad habits at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seemingly' admits the split is a play on words: novice racehorses are those not yet having won a race, not ones free of faults.
explanation.definitionFit: In racing, a horse that has not yet won a race of its type is classed among the beginners in that category.

clue.text: Ionic, as in fashion of capital

indicators.note: in fashion read as being fashioned, so the letters are shaped into a new order

explanation.surface: An architecture note on Ionic columns styled in a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ionic' and 'capital' both suggest columns (a capital tops one), but 'capital' is the city; 'in fashion' rearranges IONICAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicosia is the capital city of Cyprus.

clue.text: State footwear required for a climber

parts.note: Virginia is a US state
creepers, or brothel creepers, are thick-soled suede shoes

explanation.surface: The national government demanding boots for a mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: Brothel creepers are crepe-soled suede shoes popular with British Teddy boys in the 1950s. 'climber' is the plant, not a mountaineer.
explanation.definitionFit: A vigorous vine that clings to walls and turns red in autumn.

clue.text: Successful action of firm in court

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
a defendant up before the judge is in court

explanation.surface: A company winning its case at law.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'up' before a magistrate is to be in court on a charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A brilliant stroke or triumph, a notable victory.

parts.note: since means seeing that, because
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A question to someone named Frank about what he is looking at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name; it is the adjective meaning open and honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Honest and genuine, speaking without pretence.

clue.text: Paths within boundaries, possibly, for landing-strips

indicators.note: within says one piece sits inside the other, the path inside the boundaries

parts.note: in cricket a boundary scores runs, four or six, so boundaries may be counted as runs
a way is a path or track

explanation.surface: A question of whether footpaths lie inside the field edges, framed around airstrips.
explanation.walkthrough: A ball reaching the boundary rope in cricket scores four or six; 'possibly' admits the boundaries are only one way of scoring. 'within' puts the path inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Runways are the long paved strips on which aircraft take off and land.

clue.text: Set squares, of course, from Italy

definitions.text: Set squares, of course, from Italy

parts.words: Set squares, of course, from Italy
parts.note: set squares read as squares that have set, served as a course of a meal from Italy

explanation.surface: A geometry class receiving drawing triangles imported from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: A set square is a triangular drawing tool; here the squares are little parcels of pasta and 'course' is a dish in a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Small square pasta parcels filled with meat or cheese, an Italian dish.

indicators.note: almost says the word is not quite complete, losing its last letter

parts.note: night is the dark part of the day

explanation.surface: Evening is approaching and it is nearly dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts the final T from NIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word meaning close by, close at hand.

clue.text: Saturday's client involved in Holmes' first mystery

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A detective's weekend visitor drawn into his debut case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges all fifteen letters of SATURDAYSCLIENT.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1887 novel by Arthur Conan Doyle that introduced Sherlock Holmes.

indicators.note: tailless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a stranger is an alien, an outsider

explanation.surface: A far-off extraterrestrial without a tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alien' looks like the definition; it is the noun STRANGER, which loses its R.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange can mean cool and reserved, keeping aloof, as in a remote manner.

clue.text: Latin-derived name for Chichester, for example

definitions.text: Latin-derived name for Chichester, for example

parts.words: Latin-derived name for Chichester, for example
parts.note: Sir Francis Chichester sailed single-handed round the world; the title for such a sailor comes from Latin words for going around by ship

explanation.surface: An etymology question about the Roman name of the cathedral city of Chichester in Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: Chichester is also an English city with Roman origins, so solvers look for its Latin place name; it is the yachtsman Francis Chichester, who sailed solo round the globe in 1966-67.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor who travels all the way round the world, from Latin circum 'around' and navigare 'to sail'.

parts.note: on a golf green the pin is the flagstick marking the hole

explanation.surface: A golf picture: a quick tee shot that lands a moment from the flag.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf 'drive' and 'flag' pull toward the course, but 'Brisk drive' is a quick ride in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin is a short pleasure trip in a car, a quick outing for fun.

clue.text: I Fiend the end of god to turn me on

indicators.note: the end of picks out only the final letter of the word god
to turn tells us the letters of me on are rearranged

explanation.surface: A plea for divine help to get excited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' scrambles ME ON into EMON, placed after D, the last letter of 'god'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name an evil spirit or devil.

clue.text: Carrying cargo without having left port

indicators.note: without having says a letter is taken away from the word before

parts.note: a ship carrying cargo is laden

explanation.surface: A ship sailing loaded but without permission to leave harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the verb of departing a harbour; it is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: Aden is a seaport in Yemen at the mouth of the Red Sea.

clue.text: Give consent for silver grass to be cut short

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: cut short says the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass

explanation.surface: Permitting someone to mow silvery lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give consent for' is the definition with its preposition; 'to be cut short' drops the grass's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To say yes to something, to accept or approve it.

clue.text: First capital gains tax in Berkshire

indicators.note: gains says the first piece acquires the next, joined after it

parts.note: A is the first capital letter of the alphabet
scot is an old tax, as in scot-free

explanation.surface: Profits tax on the main city of an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Scot was an old municipal tax, surviving in 'scot-free'. Berkshire is a county west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a town in Berkshire, home of the famous racecourse.

parts.note: at can mean by, as in at the door
an ingle is a fireplace or hearth, as in inglenook

explanation.surface: Someone warm and rosy, sitting beside the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: An ingle is an old word, still found in 'inglenook', for a hearth.

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing
a spire is the pointed top of a steeple

explanation.surface: A fashionable church tower given a metal coating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Galvanise' suggests zinc plating, but here it means to rouse into action.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir someone into action or enthusiasm, to motivate.

clue.text: Titled lady of the French mating game

parts.note: du is French for of the
chess is the game that ends in checkmate

explanation.surface: An aristocratic Frenchwoman playing the dating game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mating game' suggests romance; it is chess, won by checkmate.

explanation.surface: Clubs for drivers, like motoring associations.
explanation.definitionFit: People at the wheel of cars, and long-shafted golf clubs used for tee shots.

explanation.surface: A request for help to fix a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Help given to someone, and to give a vehicle its routine maintenance check.

clue.text: Take a shine to work here in Derbyshire

parts.note: gloss is a shine on a surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take a shine to' reads as fancying something; 'Take' is only a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossop is a market town in the High Peak area of Derbyshire, in the English Midlands.

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges COSTING.
explanation.definitionFit: From the Greek gnosis, it means possessing spiritual or esoteric wisdom.

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
eyed means looked at, seen

explanation.definitionFit: Having eyes that bulge out, or wide-eyed with surprise.

indicators.note: taking says the first piece takes on the second, joined after it

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
lex is Latin for law

explanation.surface: A woman called Holly studying to be a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holly' looks like a name; it is the plant, whose botanical genus is Ilex.
explanation.definitionFit: Ilex is the botanical genus name of the evergreen shrubs with prickly leaves and red berries.

explanation.surface: Someone arriving ahead of their boss.

explanation.surface: A menu choice between meat and seafood.
explanation.definitionFit: To complain or grumble, and a freshwater fish often farmed in ponds.

indicators.note: found in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'breakwater' and 'nesting'.
explanation.definitionFit: A seabird related to gulls, with a forked tail.

indicators.note: came out suggests the letters emerging in a fresh order

explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges CAME.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point or peak of achievement.

parts.note: taking 'left' as departed, the phrase says died in a gentle, indirect way, which is the manner asked for

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually describes someone abandoned near death; read 'left' as 'departed' and 'left' is a softened way of saying 'died'.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking in a mild, indirect way to avoid saying something harsh outright.

parts.note: a jabber read as something that jabs, the device used to give jabs to patients

explanation.surface: A chatterbox talking non-stop at the doctor's surgery.

explanation.definitionFit: A hypodermic is used to inject medicine, a jab being a colloquial word for an injection.

clue.text: Was the cause of having made a fuss

explanation.surface: Blaming whoever kicked up a scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Brought about or produced; and in British slang, 'create' means to complain loudly or make a scene.
